name: crewAI

facts.description: Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents. By fostering collaborative intelligence, CrewAI empowers agents to work together seamlessly, tackling complex tasks.

title: crewAI: A Python Framework for Orchestrating Role-Playing AI Agents
answer: crewAI is an open-source Python framework, made by CrewAI Inc. under the MIT licence, for orchestrating role-playing autonomous agents that collaborate on tasks. It sits in the agent orchestration layer above language models, letting you define agents with roles, goals and backstories, give them tools, and run them as a crew or as a deterministic flow. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its production story rests on pairing flexible agents with a controlled, observable execution backbone rather than unbounded autonomy.

sections.body: crewAI is an open-source framework for building and orchestrating multi-agent AI workflows, developed by CrewAI Inc. and released under the MIT licence, with its source at github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI and its official site at crewai.com. The site describes it as a framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents, where collaborative intelligence lets agents work together on complex tasks. It is written in Python and is powered by language models, so it sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above the model itself and below the application. It does not train models or serve them; it coordinates agents that call them.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework is used for multi-step work that benefits from several specialised agents: research, analysis, drafting and review, tool and API calls, and language-heavy automations over unstructured data. Its site frames the strongest fit as tasks requiring reasoning and collaborating agents, and it lists role-based crews with specialists such as researcher, analyst and writer, shared memory and handoffs. It also covers production concerns through tracing, guardrails and an Agent Management Platform. A documented example pairs a researcher agent with Cerebras inference to produce a report on emerging technologies, and an NVIDIA integration powers agents and flows with models hosted on NVIDIA NIM microservices.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The official material is written for developers and assumes working Python, since installation is through the crewai and crewai-tools packages and examples are Python scripts. The core concepts are few and clearly named: agents with role, goal and backstory, tasks with a description and expected output, crews that combine them, a process such as sequential execution, and a kickoff call that starts the run and accepts dynamic inputs. The site offers tutorials, a developer portal, an MCP server and an llms-full.txt file for agent-ready documentation. It does not present a beginner path for people without programming experience, and it does not state formal mathematics prerequisites.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The repository has roughly 59,000 GitHub stars, and a CrewAI blog page cites 40,000 stars alongside 1.4 billion agentic automations and use by 60 percent of the Fortune 500, figures that come from the company's own marketing rather than independent measurement. The site documents integrations with Cerebras inference, NVIDIA NIM microservices and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and it links a report with insights from over 4,500 professionals building AI agents. Documentation includes a developer portal, an MCP server and llms-full.txt. The site also publishes its own 2026 State of Agentic AI survey, based on 500 executives, which is company research and should be read as such.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: crewAI is presented as serving both ends. A crew of agents with roles, tools and a sequential process can be defined in a short script and run with kickoff, which suits quick experiments. For production, the site describes Agentic Systems that combine Flows, a deterministic backbone, with intelligence deployed where it matters. Flows are described as a very thin code layer with almost no abstractions, using decorators and state management, handling conditional branching and custom business logic, event-driven and modifiable at runtime. The stated cost is architectural discipline: the site argues that prompt chains passing as agents and unbounded autonomous agents both fail in production.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site claims use by 60 percent of the Fortune 500 and cites production cases at PwC and the startup Parloa, along with DocuSign, which it says cut sales research time from hours to minutes. Its own survey reports that 81 percent of surveyed enterprises have fully adopted or are scaling agentic AI, that 57 percent prefer building on existing open-source tools, and that data readiness and insufficient talent are the top obstacles. These are vendor-published figures. Nothing in the facts or the site establishes crewAI as a legacy choice or as a universal standard, so a reader should treat it as a current, actively developed option rather than a settled default.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: crewAI is Python-first, and the site positions it against Microsoft Agent Framework, which targets .NET and Azure ecosystems, and Automation Anywhere, an enterprise RPA platform for UI and legacy system automation. It also appears in a comparison list alongside AutoGen and MetaGPT. The site's guidance is to choose crewAI for open, Python-first multi-agent crews and Microsoft Agent Framework when standardising on Azure AI services, and it notes that many enterprises use RPA for deterministic UI workflows and crewAI for cognitive, language-heavy automations. That is the polyglot pattern: a Python orchestration layer beside existing enterprise automation and cloud stacks.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid that most implementations are either too rigid or too loose, and it criticises prompt chains passing as agents, graph-based designs on maintainability grounds, and autonomous agents without architectural constraints. Token cost is a stated concern: extended reasoning can consume tens of thousands of tokens, and the site estimates that 60 to 80 percent of enterprise token spend goes to use cases that have not proven business value. What the official material does not settle is benchmarking against rival frameworks, detailed pricing, and independent verification of adoption claims. The facts also do not record a first release date, so its age cannot be stated.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
